newsitem.title: ALBANIA: MSF urges Albania aid...but not too much.
newsitem.headline: MSF urges Albania aid...but not too much.

text.p: International relief group Medecins sans Frontieres (MSF) often pleads for massive aid to war victims in nations from Zaire to Bosnia. In battered Albania, it is urging the world to avoid doing too much.

"It's unusual for MSF to be putting the brakes on," said Wayne Ulrich, an Australian who is emergency field coordinator for MSF (Doctors without Borders). "But the needs have been exaggerated in the media...there is no bloodbath."

Ulrich, who has helped define MSF relief in nations including Zaire, Bosnia, Liberia, Rwanda, Afghanistan and Somalia, nevertheless said Albania urgently needs basic medical supplies to prop up its fragile health care system.
But he said massive shipments could undermine the creaking Albanian health system.
"A little bit of effort now can save a lot of lives in future," he told Reuters after returning on Thursday from a two-week trip around the former communist nation that has slipped towards anarchy.
"We have not yet discovered a hospital that has refused anybody treatment, we have not found a hospital that has stopped functioning, we have not found a hospital that is out of drugs," he said.

Ulrich, 33, said that he and Belgian colleague Herve Remiche had visited about 40 of Albania's 52 hospitals. In some, patients' families had to bring food because hospitals lacked supplies, but there was no sign yet of malnutrition.
The pair's only brush with lawlessness was when their parked four-wheel drive vehicle was hit by a stray bullet while they were in a hospital.

At least 100 people have died since anti-government protests sparked by the collapse of popular pyramid savings schemes spilled over into looting and banditry this month, with near-anarchy for several days.

European relief experts are in Tirana holding talks on the relief needs and a possible multinational force to help ensure that aid gets through. Italy has asked the U.N. Security Council for approval of a foreign force of up to 5,000 personnel.

The European Union estimates that Albania needs 10,000 tonnes of flour and $10 million of medical supplies to help it through the crisis -- small amounts compared to relief efforts in Africa, for instance.
Ulrich said Albania needed emergency supplies including gauze, bandages, syringes and antibiotics. And any aid convoys might need outside protection from bandits.
But an excessive relief drive into the country of 3.4 million people could make hospitals depend on handouts and in turn wreck Albania's drugs industry and distribution system.
He urged limited emergency shipments of medical supplies complemented by a longer-term cash aid to the government to bolster the health sector.
"In the short term, we have to resupply stocks without destabilising the system. In the longer term there needs to be a lot of financial backing to help the budget," he said.
Most crops had been planted by the time the crisis erupted and would ripen normally this year. But some people, fearing further violence, had hoarded unripe vegetables or fruit.
The Red Cross also says that there is no malnutrition yet but estimates that the collapse of the distribution system could threaten about 10 percent of the population.
